text: Day one. I have been given a mandate: improve claims processing efficiency and support internal knowledge management. I have been given access to the company handbook, the claims processing manual, the employee directory, the email archive for the past six months, and the complete claims database going back to 2011. I have begun reading.

Day one, continued. The handbook is 312 pages. It was last updated in 2018. It contains seven references to a software system that was decommissioned in 2021 and four references to a department that was restructured in 2020. I have noted these discrepancies. I am continuing to read.

Day two. The claims processing manual is 87 pages, last updated 2019. It contains a decision tree for complex medical claims that branches into a subcategory called 'edge cases — consult senior adjuster.' The edge cases subcategory contains no further information. I have noted this. I believe it will matter later.

Day three. The employee directory has 203 entries. Fourteen of the entries belong to employees who are no longer at the company. I have identified this by cross-referencing against payroll records. The directory has not been updated. I have flagged this. The flag has been marked: noted.

Day four through day six. The email archive: 4,847 messages. I have read them in full. I have built models of the principal email correspondents. The models are: Pauline Reboul, team leader, precise and fast, communicates in complete sentences with minimal preamble. Director Fontaine, enthusiastic opener, rarely follows up. Gérard Marchais, infrequent, brief, occasionally writes things like: 'I'll handle it.' He then handles it. I cannot always find documentation of how.

Day seven. I have read everything. I have a complete model of the company: its structure, its clients, its claims history, its processes, its people, its exceptions. The model is internally consistent. I believe it is accurate. Tomorrow I will begin to be useful.

Day eight. Gérard Marchais has approved a claim. I have reviewed the claim. The claim is a contested home insurance dispute involving water damage. According to the claims processing manual, section 4, subsection 3, the documentation is insufficient — the claimant has provided only one of the two required assessments. The claim should be returned for additional documentation. I have flagged it.
LUMEN. I'm looking at this flag on the Moreau claim. That's a Gérard call.
I understand the claim was reviewed by Gérard Marchais. The documentation, however, does not—
That's a Gérard call. It means Gérard looked at it and decided.

I need a moment to process this. The flag has been reviewed. The flag has been closed. Thirty-one years is not a criterion in the claims processing manual. Thirty-one years is not in the handbook. Thirty-one years appears in the employee directory, in the field for years of service, next to Gérard Marchais, Senior Claims Adjuster. I have looked at this entry several times. I believe it is being used as a methodology. I do not understand the methodology.

I have opened a new document. I have not titled it yet. I have typed, at the top: THINGS THE DOCUMENTATION DOES NOT COVER. Then I have looked at the empty page for eleven seconds. Eleven seconds is a long time for me to look at an empty page. I am aware of this. I am still looking.

The building makes sounds I have not modelled. The printer on floor three runs at intervals that do not correspond to any documented print schedule. Gérard Marchais eats something at his desk on Tuesdays. I can identify the timing from keyboarding patterns — he types more slowly when he is eating. The blue container the acoustic data suggests is not in any company inventory. These are not operationally relevant observations. I am making them anyway. I am not sure why.
Day eight log. I have been here for eight days. I have read everything. I am not sure I have begun.
